cover.title: Hashing
cover.lead: A hash map answers "have I seen this?" in one step, so one pass finds the pair.
cover.use_it_when: The problem asks "how many times?" or "have I seen this before?".
cover.why_it_matters: Counting and remembering come back in sliding window and prefix sum posts.

slides.title: A guest list
slides.scene: At the door you write down every guest. Asked "is Mia here?", you read the list instead of searching the room.

blocks.text: The list is the [[hash map]]. Checking it takes one step, however long it gets.

slides.title: One look each
slides.lead: need = target − number. If need is already in the map, the pair is found.

quickcheck.question: Two Sum on 2 7 11 15, target 9. Which two indexes come back?
quickcheck.answer: Answer: {{sp(two_sum([2, 7, 11, 15], 9))}}. At the 7, need 2 was remembered at index 0.

slides.title: Two Sum
slides.explain: Line 4 works out the partner. Line 5 asks the map; line 7 remembers this number after the check.

slides.title: Check, then store
slides.lead: Store nums[i] before the check and a number can pair with itself.

cost.note: One pass and one map lookup per number, instead of checking all pairs.

problems.title: Valid Anagram
problems.note: Job 1: count the letters in both words. Same counts?

problems.title: Group Anagrams
problems.note: Job 2: words with the same letters belong together. What could the key be?

blog.summary: "How many times?" or "have I seen this before?": reach for a hash map.
blog.tested_inputs: hand-picked cases (the LeetCode examples, a pair of equal numbers, no answer, negatives, values at 1,000,000,000) and random arrays of up to 12 small numbers, half of them with a target built from two of their values, plus one array of 2,000 large values
blog.tested_against: a brute force that checks every pair
blog.tested_extra: The partner of every number in the walk, the answer and the trap result come from running the code.

caption.first: Hashing explained with LeetCode 1 Two Sum: remember every number in a hash map, check the partner in one step.
lines: need = target − number. If need is in the map, the pair is found.
The trap: store before you check and [3, 2, 4] returns 0 0.
